newsitem.title: JAPAN: New Tokyo shopping mall sparks tense competition.
newsitem.headline: New Tokyo shopping mall sparks tense competition.

text.p: A plan by Japan's ritzy department store operator Takashimaya Co Ltd to open a giant entertainment and shopping mall in Tokyo is sparking fierce competition among other major retailers.
Takashimaya has chosen the downtown Shinjuku district, one of the busiest shopping areas in Tokyo with 3.5 million customers per day, for its Times Square project, which opens on October 4.
"Our main purpose is to expand the Shinjuku market, which still has enormous potential," said Masato Sugita, a Takashimaya spokesman.
"Building another ordinary department store would only mean another slice of the same old pie," Sugita said. "What we needed was an innovative facility which can attract a wide range of customers."
Japan's oldest department store operator is investing 160 billion yen ($1.45 billion) in the 55,000 square metre (590,000 square feet) mall with 11 floors.

The new outlet will include the country's largest book and music stores, an indoor amusement park, five types of beauty parlours, a 3-D theatre and other attractions, in addition to regular fashion and home appliance sections.
Analysts say the coming of Takashimaya has already ignited fierce competition among retailers.

The new mall will mean a drop in sales of other department stores in Shinjuku and neighbouring areas such as Shibuya and Ikebukuro, especially during Takashimaya's first year of operation, said Tomohiro Shibahara, an analyst at the Nikko Research Centre.
Mike Allen, senior analyst of Barings Securities said: "Shinjuku's selling space will increase by 30 percent, giving a big decline in sales to surrounding stores, anywhere from seven to 15 percent."

Similarly, Futoshi Saito, senior analyst of Daiwa Institute of Research, expects a total decline of about 40 billion yen ($363 million) in the sales of Isetan and other major department stores in the area during Takashimaya's first operating year.

To counter this, nearby retailers -- there are at least five other department stores in Shinjuku, including Isetan Co Ltd and Mitsukoshi Ltd -- are expanding their selling space and introducing new brands.
"Isetan will face the least impact, maybe around seven percent," said Allen. "They have come up with an effective counterpolicy."
However, no matter how bright the prospects are for the first year of Takashimaya's new project, some analysts predict the mall will encounter problems from the second year onward.

Nikko's Shibahara said Takashimaya may even exceed its target of 80 billion yen ($727 million) in sales during its first year of operation, but it was most likely the amount would gradually wane after that.
This is because Japan's economic recovery has proved uneven, and department store sales are now facing a slow decline after hitting their peak earlier this year.
For the first time in seven months, department store sales fell 2.4 percent in July compared to a year earlier, according to a survey by the Japan Department Stores Association.

Another factor that may affect Takashimaya relates to the arrest of some company officials on suspicion of violating Japan's commercial code by paying money to racketeers to ensure the 1995 shareholders' meeting would go smoothly.
The company said this was a managerial issue and had no direct connection to its performance in Shinjuku.

However, Masahiro Matsuoka, senior analyst at Barclays de Zoete Wedd, said Takashimaya's overall performance would be somewhat affected, especially at its posh outlet in Tokyo's Nihombashi area, where corporate clients account for 30 percent of its sales.
